Guide

French drain vs. regrading: which do I need?

They solve different problems. The way water moves across your yard tells you which one you actually need.

They are not the same fix

People use drain and grading interchangeably, but they address different problems. Grading changes the shape of the ground so water flows where you want it on the surface. A drain, such as a catch basin and pipe or a French drain, collects water and carries it away underground. Many yards need a bit of both.

When you need grading

If water sheets across a wide area, sits against the slab, or the whole yard drains toward the house, the surface is shaped wrong. Regrading re-establishes fall so water runs away from the foundation and toward a real outlet. It is the right first move when the problem is broad rather than a single puddle.

When you need a drain

If water collects in one persistent low spot that will not drain, no amount of surface shaping helps, because there is nowhere for it to flow. That is a job for a catch basin and buried pipe, or a French drain where subsurface water is the issue. The water gets collected and piped to an outlet.

In clay soil, it is often both

On the heavy clay common around Baton Rouge, water does not percolate down, so subsurface French drains are less of a cure-all than they are in sandy soil. More often the fix is regrading to move surface water plus catch basins to pick up the stubborn low spots and pipe it out. The right mix depends entirely on how your yard behaves in a rain, which is exactly what a free site visit sorts out.

Common questions

Does a French drain work in Baton Rouge clay?
Sometimes, but because clay holds water at the surface, most local yards do better with regrading plus catch basins and pipe. We recommend the approach that fits how your water actually moves.
Can you tell me which I need without visiting?
The drainage diagnostic on our drainage page gives a starting read, but water is confirmed on the property, not on a screen. The site visit is free.
